docs.title: Advanced Digital Design and Verification (ADDV)
docs.text: Instructor: Sneh Saurabh Date: 12th August, 2025

docs.title: About the Course
docs.text:
Objective: - Develop a basic understanding of methods, tools, and technologies for designing and verifying complex digital systems. - Gain practical skills in advanced design and verification methodologies.

Expected Outcomes: - Apply various tasks in pre-RTL design. - Evaluate trade-offs during design stages. - Implement advanced functional verification techniques. - Design and verify systems at multiple abstraction levels using CAD tools.

docs.title: Pre-requisites
docs.text:
• VLSI Design Flow (ECE313/ECE513)
  • C++ or OOP concepts
  • Familiarity with SystemC and SystemVerilog

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Semiconductor industry (system level)
  • VLSI, CAD, FPGA, Embedded Systems, Computer Architecture
  • System-level manual design efforts and innovation areas

docs.title: Course Content Overview
docs.text:
1. Week 1: Introduction; Digital systems; Software and hardware design flows; Manufacturing and test
  2. Week 2: ESL Design – SystemC Models, TLM, Virtual Platforms, Platform-based Design
  3. Week 3: Hardware-software co-design – models, exploration, partitioning, co-simulation
  4. Week 4-5: High-level Synthesis – flow, CDFG, optimizations, scheduling, pipelining
  5. Week 6: SoC Design Methodology – IP packaging, IP-XACT, RTL generation
  6. Week 7-10: SystemVerilog, advanced simulation, formal verification, UVM, CDC/RDC
  7. Week 11-13: Power management, UPF, design flows

docs.title: Week 1 — Lecture 1: Electronic Systems & Implementation
docs.text:
Course & Lecture Info

Course: Advanced Digital Design and Verification (ADDV) Instructor: Sneh Saurabh Lecture: Week 1, Lecture 1 — Introduction to Systems, Components, and Implementation

docs.title: Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Define an electronic system and its elements.
  • Distinguish hardware, software, and other components in real systems.
  • Classify processors (fixed-behavior vs customizable) and related compute elements (coprocessors, microcontrollers, ASICs).
  • Recognize major memory categories.
  • Outline the hardware and software implementation flows.
  • Understand verification, manufacturing & test, and system integration & validation at a high level.

docs.title: 1) What is a System?
docs.text:
A system is a combination of elements that function together to produce the capability required to meet a need.

Elements may include: hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, and processes.

Electronic systems: systems designed to sense, process, and manipulate electronic signals. Examples: mobile phone, computer, robot, television, EEG machine, etc.

docs.title: System/Element relationships (concept map)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[System Need] --> B[System]
    B --> C[Elements]
    C --> C1[Hardware]
    C --> C2[Software]
    C --> C3[Equipment & Facilities]
    C --> C4[Personnel]
    C --> C5[Processes]
    B --> D[Capabilities Produced]
    D --> E[Meets the Need]

docs.title: 2) Components of Electronic Systems
docs.text:
Systems often comprise numerous subsystems built with diverse technologies; the overall functionality is richer than individual parts.

At a glance 
flowchart TD
    S["Electronic System"] --> H["Hardware"]
    S --> SW["Software"]
    S --> O["Other Components"]

    H --> H1["Processing"]
    H --> H2["Storage (Memory)"]
    H --> H3["Sensing"]
    H --> H4["Communication"]

    SW --> SW1["System SW (OS, drivers)"]
    SW --> SW2["Dev Tools (compiler, linker, debugger)"]
    SW --> SW3["Application SW (GP/Specialized)"]
    SW --> SW4["Firmware"]

    O --> O1["Packaging & PCBs"]
    O --> O2["Mechanical parts (hinges, keyboard)"]
    O --> O3["Power & Thermal"]
Key notes
  • Hardware (electronic): compute, memory, sensors/actuators, I/O and comms.
  • Software: system software, development toolchain, application software, firmware.
  • Other components: packaging, PCB, mechanical parts, power delivery, etc.

docs.title: 3) Hardware: Processor Types
docs.text:
Instruction-set/architecture determines customizability.

flowchart LR
    P[Processors] --> F[Fixed Behavior]
    P --> C[Customizable]

docs.title: 3.1 Fixed-Behavior Processors
docs.text:
• General-purpose: designed for broad computing requirements (e.g., x86, ARM cores).

  • Special-purpose: optimized for specific tasks (power, speed, area):

    • DSP processors

    • Image/vision processors

    • NPUs/TPUs (neural/tensor processing)

    • GPUs

flowchart TD
    FB[Fixed Behavior] --> GP[General Purpose CPU]
    FB --> SP[Special Purpose]
    SP --> SP1[DSP]
    SP --> SP2[Image/Video]
    SP --> SP3[NPU/TPU]
    SP --> SP4[GPU]

docs.title: 3.2 Customizable Processors
docs.text:
• ASIP (Application-Specific Instruction-set Processors): add custom instructions for domain PPA gains.

  • Configurable cores: cache sizes, pipeline depth, functional units, interfaces.

  • Commercial examples include families like Xtensa and ARC-V with full toolchains.

flowchart TD
    C["Customizable"] --> ASIP["ASIP (Extend ISA)"]
    C --> CFG["Configurable Core"]

    ASIP --> T1["Custom Instructions"]
    ASIP --> T2["Compiler/Toolchain Support"]

    CFG --> P1["Pipeline/Issue Width"]
    CFG --> P2["Cache Sizes/Hierarchy"]
    CFG --> P3["Custom Interfaces/Accelerators"]

docs.title: 4) Coprocessors
docs.text:
Definition: An auxiliary processor that supplements the main CPU for certain tasks (e.g., floating-point, graphics, signal processing, crypto, I/O, AI/vision).

Why use them?

  • Optimized for specific algorithms → better performance/Watt.

  • Let the main CPU remain simpler (can reduce cost/power in some products).

  • Over time, popular coprocessor functions may migrate into CPUs.

flowchart LR
    CPU[Main CPU] -- offload --> X1[FPU]
    CPU -- offload --> X2[GPU]
    CPU -- offload --> X3[AI/Vision]
    CPU -- offload --> X4[Crypto/Compression]
    CPU -- offload --> X5[Signal Processing]

docs.title: 5) Microcontrollers (MCUs)
docs.text:
One chip integrating CPU core(s) + memory + programmable I/O + peripherals. Often used in embedded/real-time systems (robotics, automotive, medical, IoT).

  • Typical features

    • GPIO (input mode: read sensors; output mode: drive LEDs/motors via power stages)

    • Timers/counters, watchdog

    • ADC/DAC, comparators

    • UART/SPI/I²C/CAN/etc.

    • On-chip Flash and SRAM

flowchart TB
    subgraph MCU["Microcontroller (single IC)"]
      CORE["Processor Core"]
      MEM["Flash + SRAM"]
      BUS["Internal Bus"]
      TIM["Timers / PWM"]
      GPIO["GPIO"]
      ADC["ADC / DAC"]
      COMM["UART / SPI / I2C / CAN"]
    end

    CORE -- "fetch/exec" --> MEM
    CORE <---> BUS
    BUS <---> TIM
    BUS <---> GPIO
    BUS <---> ADC
    BUS <---> COMM

    GPIO --> OUT["Actuators/Motors (via drivers)"]
    GPIO --> IN["Sensors/Buttons"]
    ADC --> SENS["Analog Sensors"]

Microcontroller vs SoC: an SoC is generally broader (may integrate multi-core CPUs, GPUs, memory controllers, etc.). An SoC can include MCU-like subsystems.

docs.title: 6) ASICs
docs.text:
Application-Specific Integrated Circuits — designed for a specific application rather than general use.

  • May integrate multiple processors, memories, accelerators, and peripherals.

  • Complex ASICs ≈ SoCs.

Example application domains

  • Networking

  • Security

  • Voice processing

  • Video encode/decode

  • Storage and I/O controllers

flowchart TB
    subgraph ASIC["ASIC / SoC (high-level)"]
      CPU1[CPU Cluster]
      ACC1[Domain Accelerator]
      MEM1[SRAM/TCAM/Cache]
      PERI[I/O Peripherals]
      BUS1[Interconnect/Fabric]
      PWR[Power/Clock/Reset]
    end
    CPU1 <--> BUS1
    ACC1 <--> BUS1
    MEM1 <--> BUS1
    PERI <--> BUS1
    PWR --> CPU1
    PWR --> ACC1
    PWR --> MEM1
    PWR --> PERI

docs.title: 7) Memory Landscape
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    M["Memory"] --> NVM["ROM (Non-Volatile)"]
    M --> VM["RAM (Volatile)"]
    M --> EXT["External Storage"]

    NVM --> PROM["PROM"]
    NVM --> EPROM["EPROM"]
    NVM --> FLASH["Flash"]

    VM --> SRAM["SRAM"]
    VM --> DRAM["DRAM"]

    EXT --> HDD["Hard Disk"]
    EXT --> ODD["Optical (CD/DVD)"]
    EXT --> USB["USB Flash"]

Notes

  • NVM/ROM: retains data without power (PROM/EPROM/Flash).

  • RAM: fast working memory (SRAM for on-chip caches; DRAM for main memory).

  • External: system-level storage devices.

docs.title: 8) Software Components
docs.text:
Categories

  • System Software: OS, device drivers, boot/firmware.

  • Software Development Tools: compiler, assembler, linker, loader, debugger, profilers, CI.

  • Application Software: end-user applications (general-purpose or domain-specific).

  • Firmware: machine instructions embedded in devices (cameras, phones, NICs, printers, routers, remotes).

flowchart LR
    SW[Software] --> SYS[System SW]
    SW --> DEV[Dev Toolchain]
    SW --> APP[Application SW]
    SW --> FWM[Firmware]

    SYS --> OS[Operating System]
    SYS --> DRV[Device Drivers]
    SYS --> BOOT[Boot / BIOS / UEFI]
    DEV --> COMP[Compiler/Assembler]
    DEV --> LINK[Linker/Loader]
    DEV --> DBG[Debugger/Profiler]
    APP --> GP[General Purpose]
    APP --> SPEC[Specialized/Domain]

docs.title: 9) Hardware + Software in a Mobile Device (conceptual)
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Phone["Mobile Phone (Conceptual Stack)"]
      subgraph HW["Hardware"]
        RF["RF Front-end"]
        AP["Application Processor / SoC"]
        MEM["LPDDR / eMMC / UFS"]
        PER["Peripherals: Sensor, Display, Camera, Audio, BT/WiFi"]
        PWR["PMIC/Battery"]
      end
      subgraph SWStack["Software"]
        K["Linux Kernel / RTOS"]
        HAL["Hardware Abstraction Layer"]
        SS["System Services & Daemons"]
        RT["Runtime (e.g., Android Runtime)"]
        API["System APIs"]
        APP["Apps (System/Privileged/3rd-party)"]
      end
    end

    HW --> SWStack
    API --> APP
    SS --> RT
    HAL --> K
    K --> AP
    AP --> MEM
    AP --> PER

docs.title: 10) System Implementation — Bird’s-Eye View
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    SF[System Functionality / Requirements] --> PART[Partitioning]
    PART --> HWF[HW Functionality]
    PART --> SWF[SW Functionality]
    HWF --> IC[IC Design & Fabrication]
    IC --> FAB[Fabricated ICs/SoCs/Peripherals]
    SWF --> SWDEV[Software Development]
    SWDEV --> EXE[Executables: Firmware, Drivers, Apps]
    FAB --> INT[System Integration, Validation & Test]
    EXE --> INT
    INT --> PROD[Product]

Project-level actions

  1. Map functionality to HW vs SW.

  2. Build components A. HW design, verification, fabrication B. SW development

  3. Integrate and validate the combined system.

docs.title: 11) Hardware Design Implementation
docs.text:
Two major transformations:

  • Logic Synthesis: Convert RTL → equivalent netlist (in target library).

  • Physical Design: Convert netlist → layout (GDS) ready for fabrication.

flowchart LR
    RTL["RTL"] --> SYN["Logic Synthesis"]
    SYN --> NET["Gate-level Netlist"]
    NET --> PD["Physical Design"]
    PD --> LAYOUT["Layout (GDS)"]
    LAYOUT --> FAB["Fabrication"]

Typical physical design tasks

flowchart TB
    A[Netlist] --> B[Chip Planning / Floorplanning]
    B --> C[Placement]
    C --> D[Clock Tree Synthesis]
    D --> E[Global Routing]
    E --> F[Detailed Routing]
    F --> G[ECO/Design Fixes]
    G --> H[Write GDS]

docs.title: 12) Hardware Design Verification
docs.text:
Goal: Ensure the design implements the intended functionality under constraints. Performed at multiple stages of the VLSI flow.

  • Functional Verification

    • Simulation-based (directed, random, constrained random, coverage-driven)

    • Formal methods (property checking, model checking)

    • Equivalence checking (e.g., RTL vs netlist)

  • Physical Verification

    • DRC, ERC, LVS

    • Signal integrity, IR drop, timing (STA), variation analysis

    • Sign-off checks

flowchart TD
    V[Verification] --> FV[Functional Verification]
    V --> PV[Physical Verification]
    FV --> SIM[Simulation-based]
    FV --> FORM[Formal Methods]
    FV --> EQ[Equivalence Checking]
    PV --> DRC[DRC/ERC/LVS]
    PV --> STA[STA & Timing Reports]
    PV --> SI[SI/IR drop/EM]

docs.title: 13) Hardware Manufacturing & Test
docs.text:
Input: Final GDS from physical design. Output: Chips that pass production test.

flowchart TD
    G[GDS] --> PRE[Pre-process & Mask Prep]
    PRE --> WAF[Wafer Fabrication]
    WAF --> DIE[Die Testing]
    DIE --> PKG[Packaging]
    PKG --> FT[Final Testing]
    FT --> CHIP[Chips Shipped]

Device-level test loop (ATE)

flowchart LR
    TP[Test Patterns] --> DIEU[Die Under Test]
    ER[Expected Responses] --> CMP{Match?}
    DIEU --> AR[Actual Responses]
    AR --> CMP
    ER --> CMP
    CMP -- Yes --> PASS[Test Pass / Accept]
    CMP -- No --> FAIL[Test Fail / Reject/Diagnose]

docs.title: 14) Software Development Process
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    PLAN["Planning & Requirement Analysis"] --> ARCH["Designing Architecture"]
    ARCH --> CODE["Implementation / Coding"]
    CODE --> TEST["Testing (manual & automated)"]
    TEST --> DEP["Deployment & Integration"]
    DEP --> MAINT["Maintenance (bug fixes, enhancements, support)"]

  • Planning: resources, schedules, functional and technical definitions, documentation.

  • Architecture: layers, modules, responsibilities, technology selection.

  • Implementation: compilers/interpreters, build systems, debuggers used to produce executables.

  • Testing: unit/integration/system/regression; automation & CI.

  • Deployment: delivery to target environment; integration with other components.

  • Maintenance: fixes, performance optimization, new features.

docs.title: 15) System Integration & Validation
docs.text:
Integration begins as components become available. It surfaces interface/integration issues early.

  • Validation highlights

    • Run actual OS/applications on fabricated silicon or accurate platforms.

    • Exercise system-level scenarios not covered in unit tests.

    • Find electrical issues (crosstalk, IR drop, thermal, variation).

    • Stress/soak tests and corner/abuse cases.

flowchart TD
    FAB[Fabricated HW/Platform] --> INT[System Integration]
    EXE[SW: Firmware/Drivers/Apps] --> INT
    INT --> VAL[Validation]
    VAL --> PROD[Ship Product]

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Electronic systems combine hardware + software + other disciplines to meet a defined need.

  • Compute choices range from fixed-behavior CPUs/accelerators to customizable ASIPs.

  • MCUs integrate compute + peripherals on one die for embedded control; ASICs/SoCs tailor whole chips to applications.

  • The VLSI flow transforms RTL → netlist → layout while verification ensures correctness.

  • Manufacturing & ATE confirm defect-free parts; integration/validation demonstrates end-to-end behavior.

docs.title: References & Further Reading
docs.text: • Saurabh, S. (2023). Introduction to VLSI Design Flow. Cambridge University Press.

docs.title: Week 1 – Lecture 2: Electronic System Level (ESL) Design
docs.text: Course: Advanced Digital Design and Verification Instructor: Sneh Saurabh • Date: 14 Aug 2025

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Move up the abstraction stack (ESL) to fight SoC complexity.
  • Create an executable specification → analyze → partition HW/SW → implement → verify → iterate.
  • Use TLM, SystemC, VIPs, and HLS/ISS/virtual platforms to accelerate design + verification.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Why RTL-first breaks in modern SoCs

  • More features, more HW+SW, more comms → time ↑, cost ↑, FoM compromises.
  • Strict time-to-market makes long RTL cycles risky.

Counter-move

  • Higher-level abstraction (ESL) to boost design efficiency and parallelize HW/SW development.

Effects vs Fix

Pain ESL Relief Long design time Early modeling + architectural exploration Costly late changes Fast iteration at high abstraction FoM compromises Early analysis of power/area/perf trade-offs Verification bottlenecks Co-verification, VIPs, mixed-abstraction TBs

docs.title: What is ESL?
docs.text:
A higher-level executable abstraction of the system that is above RTL, aimed at comprehension, exploration, and early verification.

Expectations

  • Time-to-result ↓, FoM ↑, cost-effective, concurrent HW/SW development.

docs.title: Abstraction contrast
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  spec["Specification"]
  rtl["RTL (HDL)"]
  gds["Layout (GDS)"]
  esl["ESL"]

  spec -- Manual Effort --> rtl;
  rtl --> gds;
  spec -- ESL Modeling --> esl;
  esl --> rtl;

  classDef low fill:#eeeeee,stroke:#999,color:#333;
  class rtl,gds low;

````

---

## ESL Flow (big picture)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Specification]
    M[ESL Model]
    A[Analyze]
    F{Acceptable?}
    P[Partition]
    SW[SW Model]
    HW[HW Model]
    D[Analyze & Debug]
    OK[Acceptable]
    SI[SW Implementation]
    HI[HW Implementation]
    PV[Post-Partitioning Verification]
    MOD[Modify]

    S-->M-->A-->F
    F -- "No" --> MOD --> M
    F -- "Yes" --> P
    P --> SW --> D
    P --> HW --> D
    D -->|Refine| SW
    D -->|Refine| HW
    D --> OK
    OK --> SI & HI --> PV
    PV -->|Issues| MOD

docs.title: Decisions & Deliverables at ESL
docs.text:
• Architectural exploration/estimation/optimization

    • Concurrency: sequential / parallel / pipelined / multithreaded

    • Communication: bus / buffered / memory / point-to-point

    • Functional adequacy: algorithm choice, arbitration, data representation (fixed vs float)

  • HW–SW partitioning with fewer experiments

  • Parallel SW development before HW exists

  • IP & HW–SW integration

  • RTL generation

  • Faster verification (mixed abstraction, auto TB scaffolding)

docs.title: Specifications & Executable Specs
docs.text:
What counts as an executable spec?

  • A runnable functional/behavioral model that exhibits intended behavior.
  • Tech: SystemC, TLM, SystemVerilog, MATLAB, XML, IP-XACT, SDL.

docs.title: Levels of executable spec
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  AS["Architecture Spec\n(ISA, behaviors, features)"]
  DS["Design Spec\n(uarch: pipeline, caches, counts)"]
  TLM["Transaction-Level Modeling\n(bus transactions, timing options)"]

  AS --> DS --> TLM

Good spec attributes

  • Complete & precise functional requirements + constraints
  • Avoid premature platform details
  • Evolves with refinement; supports mixing abstraction levels
  • Source of truth for requirements → implementation → verification

docs.title: Analysis & Modifications at ESL
docs.text:
• Pre-partition: time/space/power/complexity/TTM trade-offs

  • Static: maintainability, usability, criticality, reliability

  • Dynamic: latency/throughput, arbitration/scheduling effects

  • Reqs for analysis: computation (fixed/float), comms (bandwidth)

docs.title: Partitioning (HW vs SW)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  E["Executable Spec"] --> C{"Criteria"};

  C -->|Perf target| HW1["HW Candidate"];
  C -->|Flexibility| SW1["SW Candidate"];
  C -->|Area/Power| HW2["Accelerator"];
  C -->|Safety/Security| HW3["Isolated IP"];
  C -->|Reuse| SW2["FW / Driver"];

  HW1 --> HWAs["HW Subsystem"];
  HW2 --> HWAs;
  HW3 --> HWAs;

  SW1 --> SWAs["SW Subsystem"];
  SW2 --> SWAs;

  HWAs --> IF["Defined Interfaces (TLM/AMBA/etc)"];
  SWAs --> IF;

Decide also:

  • Memory org: ROM/SRAM/DRAM/…

  • Interconnect/communication scheme

  • Sub-partitioning across multiple CPUs and multiple HW teams

docs.title: and type of processors (and potential ISA changes)
Post-partitioning: Analysis, Debug, Verification
docs.text:
• Analysis: performance, interfaces, area, cost, debugability

  • Debug: run SW on ISS; model HW with SystemC/HDL; ensure interface compatibility

  • Verification planning @ higher abstraction:

    • Coverage at TLM

    • Assertions/properties at the same level

    • Mixed-abstraction environments (e.g., TLM + RTL)

  • Iterate if intent not preserved.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Spec
    participant ESL
    participant Part as Partition
    participant SW as SW Model/ISS
    participant HW as HW Model/RTL
    participant Ver as Post-Part Verify
    Spec->>ESL: Executable spec
    ESL->>Part: Analyze & Partition
    Part->>SW: Build SW model
    Part->>HW: Build HW model
    SW-->>Ver: Stimulus/Results
    HW-->>Ver: Stimulus/Results
    Ver-->>ESL: Issues? -> Modify & Iterate

docs.title: Waterfall (pre-ESL)
docs.text: • Linear, sequential; late feedback.

docs.title: Spiral (with ESL)
docs.text:
• Iterative, risk-driven; SW & HW co-evolve.
gantt
    dateFormat  X
    title Waterfall vs Spiral (conceptual)
    section Waterfall
    Requirements   :a1, 1, 2
    Design         :a2, 3, 2
    Implement      :a3, 5, 2
    Integrate/Test :a4, 7, 2
    section Spiral (overlapping)
    Prototype/Model(ESL)   :b1, 1, 1
    Risk Analysis          :b2, 2, 1
    Build/Refine           :b3, 2, 2
    Evaluate/Plan Next     :b4, 4, 1
    Next Spiral            :b5, 5, 3

docs.title: Applying ESL to Software
docs.text:
• Generate SW from ESL or refined models (software synthesis) or hand-code guided by the model.

  • Observability into HW via models.

  • Scope

    • ISS: CPU regs/mem visible

    • Virtual Platform: full SoC (user I/F, storage, accelerators)

  • Exec platforms: workstation, FPGA-based emulation

  • Metrics: speed, memory footprint

flowchart LR
  SSW["Software"];
  ISS["Hardware Model (ISS)"];
  VP(("Virtual Platform"));

  SSW <--> ISS;
  SSW --> VP;
  ISS --> VP;

docs.title: Debuggability
docs.text: Approach Pros Cons HW trace buffers Real silicon visibility Area/perf cost, security concerns ESL-based PC/data trace from models, no HW cost Model fidelity limits, discipline

docs.title: Hardware Implementation Paths
docs.text:
• RTL to gates via synthesis.

Options

  1. Extensible processors (custom instructions, SIMD/MAC) + vendor toolchains

  2. Co-processors (DSP/VLIW attached on bus)

  3. ASIC (HLS from C/C++/SystemC → RTL)

  4. FPGA (rapid prototyping; same HLS path)

graph LR
    H[ESL/C/C++/SystemC] --> HLS[High-Level Synthesis]
    HLS --> RTL[RTL]
    RTL --> ASIC[ASIC Flow]
    RTL --> FPGA[FPGA Flow]

docs.title: Implementation Verification
docs.text:
• Verify implementation preserves design intent (compare to post-partition model).

  • Speed tricks: subsystem-level focus, mixed abstraction, FPGA prototypes.

  • Pass/Fail notions

    • Positive: requirement satisfied (valid inputs)

    • Negative: robustness (invalid inputs)

docs.title: Verification IPs (VIPs)
docs.text:
• Reusable verification components.
flowchart LR
    VIP[Verification IP]
    VIP -->|Dynamic| Dyn[Stimulus, Scoreboard, Coverage]
    VIP -->|Static| Sta[Assertions/Properties]

docs.text:
timeline
    title SystemC Key Milestones
    1996 : Development starts

docs.title: Why SystemC?
docs.text:
• Bridges SW/HW; models parallelism in familiar C++.

  • Any valid C++ program is valid SystemC (it’s an extension).

  • Heavy use of templates/macros/libs.

docs.title: Simulation Pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  Dev["C++ Dev Env"];
  Comp["Compile"];
  LinkStep["Link"];
  Exe["Executable"];
  RunStep["Run on Host (Win/Unix)"];
  Result["Simulation Results"];

  Dev --> Comp;
  Comp --> LinkStep;
  LinkStep --> Exe;
  Exe --> RunStep;
  RunStep --> Result;

docs.title: SystemC “Hello, World!”
docs.text:
#include <systemc.h>

SC_MODULE(Hello_SystemC) {
    SC_CTOR(Hello_SystemC) {
        SC_THREAD(module_thread); // register thread process
    }
    void module_thread() {
        SC_REPORT_INFO("Module Thread Saying", "Hello SystemC World!");
    }
};

int sc_main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    Hello_SystemC HelloWorld_i("HelloWorld_i"); // create instance
    sc_start();                                  // start simulator (run to time 0 unless events)
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Compile (example)
docs.text:
# from the directory with main.cpp
g++ -I<path_to_systemc_include> -L<path_to_systemc_lib> main.cpp -lsystemc -o hello_sc
./hello_sc

Checklist before compiling

  • g++ installed
  • -I points to systemc/include
  • -L points to the lib directory (e.g., lib-linux64)
  • Link with -lsystemc
  • If runtime can’t find the shared lib, set LD_LIBRARY_PATH (Linux) or use rpath.

docs.title: Quick Study Guide
docs.text:

docs.title: Week 2 — Lecture 1: SystemC
docs.text:
Course: Advanced Digital Design and Verification Instructor: Sneh Saurabh • Date: 19 Aug 2025 Topic: SystemC basics, toolchain, simulation kernel, processes, and data types

Key Takeaways

  • SystemC = C++ library + discrete‑event kernel. You write C++ that models hardware structure & behavior with time.
  • Simulation phases: Elaboration → Execution (delta cycles & time) → Cleanup.
  • Modules contain ports, channels/signals, and processes (SC_METHOD, SC_THREAD, SC_CTHREAD).
  • Build with g++ (or MSVC/Clang), link libsystemc, ensure loader finds it (env LD_LIBRARY_PATH/DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH or rpath).
  • Numeric/logic families provide bit‑accurate arithmetic and four‑valued logic (0,1,X,Z). Use the closest type that satisfies semantics.
  • Time API: sc_time, wait(), events & notifications, time resolution and default unit control precision.

docs.title: 0) High‑level map
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  SC[SystemC] --> ST[Structure]
  SC --> BH[Behavior]
  SC --> TM[Time]
  ST --> MOD[SC_MODULE]
  ST --> PRT[Ports]
  ST --> CH[Channels/Signals]
  BH --> PR1[SC_METHOD]
  BH --> PR2[SC_THREAD]
  BH --> PR3[SC_CTHREAD]
  CH --> SIG[sc_signal<T>]
  CH --> FIFO[sc_fifo<T>]
  CH --> MUT[sc_mutex]
  PRT --> IF[Interfaces]
  TM --> EVT[Events]
  TM --> W[wait()] 
  TM --> TS[sc_time]

docs.title: 1) What is SystemC?
docs.text:
SystemC is a - C++ class library providing types (bit‑vectors, fixed‑point, events, clocks, channels) and macros (e.g., SC_MODULE). - An event‑driven kernel that schedules processes and advances time.

classDiagram
  class Kernel {
    +delta_cycle
    +evaluate()
    +update()
    +next_event_time()
  }
  class SC_MODULE {
    +ports
    +channels
    +processes
  }
  class SC_METHOD
  class SC_THREAD
  class SC_CTHREAD
  Kernel <.. SC_METHOD : schedules
  Kernel <.. SC_THREAD : schedules
  Kernel <.. SC_CTHREAD : schedules
  SC_MODULE o-- SC_METHOD
  SC_MODULE o-- SC_THREAD
  SC_MODULE o-- SC_CTHREAD

docs.title: 2.1 Source (main.cpp)
docs.text:
#include <systemc.h>

SC_MODULE(Hello_SystemC) {
  SC_CTOR(Hello_SystemC) { SC_THREAD(module_thread); }
  void module_thread() {
    SC_REPORT_INFO("Hello", "Module Thread Saying:: Hello SystemC World!");
  }
};

int sc_main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
  Hello_SystemC hello_i("hello_i");
  sc_start();
  return 0;
}

docs.title: 2.2 Build & run (Linux, shared)
docs.text:
# Compile
g++ -std=c++17 -I${SYSTEMC_HOME}/include -c main.cpp

# Link
g++ -L${SYSTEMC_HOME}/lib-linux64 -lsystemc -lpthread -o a.out main.o

# Loader (option A): env var
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=${SYSTEMC_HOME}/lib-linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

# or (option B): bake rpath into executable
# g++ ... -Wl,-rpath,${SYSTEMC_HOME}/lib-linux64 -lsystemc -lpthread -o a.out

./a.out

sequenceDiagram
  participant Dev as Developer
  participant CC as g++
  participant Link as Linker
  participant Ldr as Runtime Loader
  Dev->>CC: compile main.cpp (-I include)
  CC-->>Dev: main.o
  Dev->>Link: link main.o (-L ... -lsystemc -lpthread)
  Link-->>Dev: a.out
  Dev->>Ldr: run a.out (LD_LIBRARY_PATH set)
  Ldr-->>Dev: SystemC banner + INFO message

docs.title: 2.3 Static vs Dynamic linking
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  subgraph Static@build
    X[Objects] -->|archive| LA[libsystemc.a]
    APP[App] -->|link + copy code| EXE[a.out (fat)]
  end
  subgraph Dynamic@run
    Y[Objects] -->|link stubs| EXE2[a.out (slim)]
    EXE2 -->|needs| SO[libsystemc.so]
    SO -->|found by| PATH[LD_LIBRARY_PATH or rpath]
  end

docs.title: 3) Simulation lifecycle & delta cycles
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant K as Kernel
  participant P as Processes (ready)
  participant Q as Update Queue
  Note over K: t = 0, delta = 0
  K->>P: evaluate() (all sensitive/triggered)
  P-->>Q: request signal updates/events
  K->>Q: update() (commit signal writes)
  K-->>K: if more events in same time -> delta++ and repeat
  alt no more events at t
    K-->>K: advance time to next scheduled event
  end
  • Elaboration (C++ constructor time): build module hierarchy, bind ports↔channels, register processes, compute static sensitivities.
  • Execution: repeated evaluate → update → delta++ until no events remain, then jump to next time.
  • Cleanup: destruct objects, print reports.

docs.title: 4.1 Process matrix
docs.text: Process Can wait()? Typical use Sensitivity Notes SC_METHOD ❌ combinational sensitive << sig / next_trigger() runs to completion; default calls once at time 0 unless dont_initialize() SC_THREAD ✅ timed/stateful wait(evt) / wait(delay) coroutine; use loops; can wait(N, SC_NS) SC_CTHREAD ✅ (implicit clock) synchronous pipelines sensitive << clk.pos()/neg() via reset_signal_is() use wait() per cycle; reset style via reset_signal_is()

docs.title: 4.2 Sensitivity rules
docs.text:
• Static lists: declared at elaboration (SC_METHOD + sensitive << a << b;).
  • Dynamic: next_trigger(evt | delay) inside METHODS changes sensitivity for next invocation only.
  • dont_initialize() stops the first call at time 0.
  • SC_THREAD/SC_CTHREAD start suspended until first wait(...) completes.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Sleeping
  Sleeping --> Ready: event or time triggers
  Ready --> Running: scheduled by kernel
  Running --> Sleeping: end of METHOD or `wait()` in THREAD

docs.title: 5) Channels, ports, interfaces
docs.text:
classDiagram
  class sc_interface { <<abstract>> +methods }
  class sc_port~IF~ { +bind(IF) }
  class sc_signal~T~ { +read() +write(T) }
  class sc_fifo~T~ { +read() +write(T) +num_available() }
  sc_signal ..|> sc_interface
  sc_fifo ..|> sc_interface
  sc_port o-- sc_interface

Binding rules - One port binds to one interface (or a vector of ports binds one‑by‑one). - Directional convenience ports: sc_in<T>, sc_out<T>, sc_inout<T> wrap sc_port. - Multiple readers/writers: allowed by channel semantics (e.g., sc_signal allows 1 writer; multiple writers require a resolved channel).

docs.title: 6) Time API
docs.text:
• sc_time t(10, SC_NS);
  • wait(10, SC_NS), wait(evt), wait(evt | t).
  • Global configuration: 
    sc_set_time_resolution(1, SC_PS);
sc_set_default_time_unit(1, SC_NS);

sequenceDiagram
  participant T as SC_THREAD
  participant K as Kernel
  T->>K: wait(5, SC_NS)
  K-->>T: resume at t0+5ns
  T->>K: evt.notify(10, SC_NS)
  T->>K: wait(evt)
  K-->>T: resume when event fires

Event notification - Immediate: notify() (next delta). - Timed: notify(dt) schedules in future time.

docs.title: 7) Data types (namespace sc_dt)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  DT[Types] --> L[Logic]
  DT --> N[Numeric]
  L --> L1[sc_logic (0,1,Z,X)]
  L --> L2[sc_bv<W> 2‑valued]
  L --> L3[sc_lv<W> 4‑valued]
  N --> I1[sc_int<W>]
  N --> I2[sc_uint<W>]
  N --> I3[sc_bigint<W>]
  N --> I4[sc_biguint<W>]
  N --> F1[sc_fixed<W,I> / sc_ufixed<W,I>]
  N --> F2[sc_fix / sc_ufix]
  N --> FF[sc_fix_fast / sc_ufix_fast]

Selections & concatenation 

sc_uint<4> a = 0xA;         // 1010
sc_uint<4> b = 0x3;         // 0011
sc_uint<8> cat = (a, b);    // 1010_0011

sc_uint<4> y = 0;
y.range(3,1) = 0b111;       // y = 1110
bool b0 = (y[0] == 0);

Fixed‑point essentials 

sc_fixed<5,3>  weight = 1.5;   // W=5, I=3 (signed)
sc_ufixed<8,6> price  = 12.25; // W=8, I=6 (unsigned)

// Runtime‑configurable
sc_fix  bias(5,3);             // W=5, I=3
sc_ufix dist(8,2);

Quantization / Overflow (when using full fixed‑point types) - Quantization modes: SC_TRN, SC_TRN_ZERO, SC_RND, SC_RND_ZERO, SC_RND_MIN_INF, SC_RND_INF, SC_RND_CONV. - Overflow modes: SC_WRAP, SC_WRAP_SM, SC_SAT, SC_SAT_ZERO, SC_SAT_SYM.

Performance

SystemC types are implemented as classes; arithmetic is slower than native C++. Use the narrowest accurate type, and prefer sc_uint/sc_int over big/fixed types unless required.

docs.title: 8) Tracing & reporting
docs.text:
sc_trace_file* tf = sc_create_vcd_trace_file("wave");
sc_trace(tf, clk, "clk");
sc_trace(tf, d.cnt, "cnt");
sc_start(200, SC_NS);
sc_close_vcd_trace_file(tf);
  • SC_REPORT_INFO/WARNING/ERROR/FATAL with categories; filter via sc_report_handler.
  • VCD grows fast; trace only what you inspect.

docs.title: 9) Build systems (beyond one‑liners)
docs.text:
CMake 

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(hello_systemc CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(SYSTEMC_HOME $ENV{SYSTEMC_HOME})
include_directories(${SYSTEMC_HOME}/include)
link_directories(${SYSTEMC_HOME}/lib-linux64)
add_executable(hello main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(hello systemc pthread)
# rpath so you don't need LD_LIBRARY_PATH
set_target_properties(hello PROPERTIES INSTALL_RPATH "${SYSTEMC_HOME}/lib-linux64")

Windows notes - Use MSVC or MSYS2/Clang. Link systemc.lib; the runtime DLL must be on PATH. - Replace -lpthread with appropriate Windows threading lib (SystemC for Windows usually bundles it).

docs.title: 10) Common pitfalls & fixes
docs.text: Symptom Root cause Fix error while loading shared libraries: libsystemc.so Loader can’t see shared lib Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH or use linker rpath Undefined refs to sc_* Forgot -lsystemc or wrong -L Add correct -L dir and -lsystemc -lpthread ABI mismatch SystemC built with different compiler/flags Rebuild SystemC or match toolchain Multiple writers to sc_signal Channel semantics violated Use resolved channel or arbitration SC_METHOD using wait() Illegal in methods Convert to SC_THREAD or use next_trigger()

docs.title: 11) Mini testbench skeleton
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(tb) {
  sc_clock clk{"clk", 10, SC_NS};
  sc_signal<bool> rst;
  DUT* dut{nullptr};
  SC_CTOR(tb) {
    dut = new DUT("dut");
    dut->clk(clk);
    SC_THREAD(stim);  // drive reset, inputs
  }
  void stim(){
    rst = 1; wait(2, SC_NS); rst = 0; // etc.
    wait(1, SC_US);
    sc_stop();
  }
};

docs.title: 12) Checklist
docs.text:
• Install SystemC; set ${SYSTEMC_HOME}
  • Build & run Hello SystemC
  • Draw module ↔ process ↔ channel diagrams (see above)
  • Choose types; justify widths/precision
  • Add VCD tracing & at least one SC_REPORT_*
  • Add stimuli + self‑check + basic CI build (CMake)

docs.text:

docs.title: Week 2 — Lecture 2: SystemC
docs.text:
Course: Advanced Digital Design and Verification Instructor: Sneh Saurabh • Date: 21 Aug 2025 Topic: Modules, processes, events, signals, and notifications in SystemC

Key Takeaways

  • Modules (SC_MODULE) are the building blocks of SystemC; contain ports, channels, processes, and other members.
  • Constructors (SC_CTOR) initialize and connect sub‑designs, register processes, and set sensitivities.
  • Processes can be SC_METHOD or SC_THREAD, with different rules for suspension and persistence.
  • Simulation involves evaluate/update cycles; kernel is cooperative multitasking.
  • Events (sc_event) allow synchronization between processes; used with notify() and wait().
  • Sensitivity can be static (declared at elaboration) or dynamic (changed at runtime).
  • Signals (sc_signal<T>) follow the evaluate/update model and embody delta cycles.
  • Notifications can be immediate or delayed (after update phase).

docs.title: 1) Modules
docs.text:
classDiagram
  class SC_MODULE {
    +ports
    +channels
    +submodules
    +processes
    +constructor()
    +destructor()
  }

  SC_MODULE <|-- UserModule

  class SC_CTOR {
    +alloc_subdesigns()
    +connect_subdesigns()
    +register_processes()
    +set_sensitivity()
  }
  • Modules are C++ classes inheriting from sc_module.
  • Organized as .h for declaration, .cpp for implementation.
  • Contain: constructor, ports, submodules, channels, member data, processes.

docs.title: 2) Module constructor
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(my_mod) {
  SC_CTOR(my_mod) : init_list {
    // allocate submodules
    // connect ports ↔ channels
    // register processes with kernel
    // set sensitivity
  }
};

flowchart TB
  A[Constructor] --> B[Allocate submodules]
  A --> C[Connect submodules]
  A --> D[Register processes]
  A --> E[Set static sensitivity]
  A --> F[Misc setup]

docs.title: 3) Module hierarchy
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(Bottom) {
  SC_CTOR(Bottom) { cout << name() << endl; }
};

SC_MODULE(Mid) {
  Bottom b1, b2;
  SC_CTOR(Mid) : b1("b1"), b2("b2") {}
};

SC_MODULE(Top) {
  Mid mid;
  Bottom b;
  SC_CTOR(Top) : mid("mid"), b("b") {}
};

flowchart TB
  Top --> Mid
  Top --> B
  Mid --> B1
  Mid --> B2
  • Instances of submodules are declared as data members of the parent.
  • new/delete operators can create/destroy modules dynamically.

docs.title: 4) Simulation processes
docs.text:
• Kernel schedules execution; cooperative, non‑preemptive.
  • Registered via SC_THREAD or SC_METHOD.
Property SC_THREAD SC_METHOD Suspension wait() allowed Cannot wait(); uses next_trigger() Behavior Like software thread, persistent state Like function, no persistence Registration SC_THREAD(func) SC_METHOD(func) 
classDiagram
  class SC_THREAD {
    +persistent vars
    +suspension via wait()
  }
  class SC_METHOD {
    +no persistence
    +reactive to sensitivity
  }

docs.title: 5) Process syntax example
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(proc) {
  void th(){ while(1){ cout<<"th @"<<sc_time_stamp(); wait(500,SC_MS);} }
  void me(){ cout<<"me @"<<sc_time_stamp(); next_trigger(200,SC_MS);}
  SC_CTOR(proc){ SC_THREAD(th); SC_METHOD(me); }
};
  • th prints every 500 ms.
  • me prints every 200 ms.
  • Simulation ends at 1500 ms.

docs.title: 6) Simulation engine
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[Elaboration] --> B[Initialize]
  B --> C[Evaluate]
  C --> D[Update]
  D -->|if events| C
  D -->|else| E[Advance Time]
  E --> B
  E -->|if none| F[Cleanup]
  • Evaluate/Update: all runnable processes execute one at a time.
  • Processes return by end of function or wait().
  • Delta cycles = repeated evaluate/update at same time.

docs.title: 7) Events
docs.text:
• sc_event represents a zero‑time notification.
  • Has no value and no duration.
  • Trigger: event.notify().
  • Wait: wait(event).
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as Thread A
  participant E as Event
  participant M as Thread B
  T->>E: notify()
  M->>E: wait(event)
  E-->>M: resumes immediately or scheduled

docs.title: 8) Event example
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(two) {
  sc_event given, taken;
  void give(){ while(1){ wait(500,SC_MS); cout<<"given"<<sc_time_stamp(); taken.notify(100,SC_MS);} }
  void take(){ while(1){ wait(given); cout<<"taken"<<sc_time_stamp(); }}
  SC_CTOR(two){ SC_THREAD(give); SC_THREAD(take); }
};
  • Two threads coordinate via events.
  • give notifies taken after 100 ms.
  • take waits for given.

docs.title: 9) Sensitivity
10) Signals
docs.text:
• Primitive channel sc_signal<T> implements evaluate/update.
  • Two values: current and new.
  • write(T) = schedule new value.
  • read() = fetch current value.
flowchart LR
  P1[Process 1] -->|write(x)| SIG[sc_signal]
  SIG -->|visible after update| P2[Process 2]

docs.title: 11) Signal member functions
docs.text:
• value_changed_event(): returns event triggered on update.
  • event(): check if change happened in last delta cycle.
  • Special events for sc_signal<bool> and sc_signal<sc_logic>:
  • posedge_event(), negedge_event().
  • sc_buffer<T>: like signal but event fires on every write.

docs.title: 12) Immediate vs Delayed notification
docs.text:
Type Function Effect Immediate notify() triggers before update Delayed notify(SC_ZERO_TIME) triggers after update (next delta) 
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Process
  participant E as Event
  P->>E: notify()
  Note over E: Immediate, before update
  P->>E: notify(SC_ZERO_TIME)
  Note over E: Scheduled after update

docs.title: 13) References
docs.text: • Black, David C., and Jack Donovan, SystemC: From the ground up. Springer, 2004.

docs.title: Week 3 — Lecture 1: SystemC
docs.text:
Course: Advanced Digital Design and Verification Instructor: Sneh Saurabh • Date: 26 Aug 2025 Topic: Communication in SystemC: Interfaces, Ports, Channels, and Testbenches

Key Takeaways

  • Communication in SystemC is modeled using interfaces, ports, and channels, enabling modular and reusable design.
  • Interfaces define what services are provided (abstract methods); channels define how those services are implemented.
  • Ports allow modules to access channels without knowing the implementation, maintaining encapsulation.
  • sc_port, sc_export, and specialized ports (sc_in, sc_out, sc_inout) provide flexible modeling constructs.
  • Testbenches in SystemC simulate complete systems by driving inputs and observing outputs, allowing debugging via waveforms and VCD dumps.

docs.title: 1.1 Interfaces (Abstract Services)
docs.text:
• An interface is an abstract class derived from sc_interface.
  • Provides pure virtual functions — must be implemented by a channel.
  • Interfaces decouple communication definition from implementation.
class my_interface : public sc_interface {
public:
  virtual int read(void) = 0;   // service 1
  virtual void write(int i) = 0; // service 2
};

docs.title: 1.2 Channels (Concrete Implementations)
docs.text:
• A channel is a class that derives from sc_channel or sc_prim_channel.
  • Implements all abstract methods of the interface.
  • Can store state (e.g., data variables).
class my_channel : public sc_prim_channel, public my_interface {
  int data;
public:
  int read(void) override { return data; }
  void write(int i) override { data = i; }
};

classDiagram
  class sc_interface {
    <<abstract>>
    +pure virtual methods
  }
  class my_interface
  class sc_prim_channel
  class my_channel

  sc_interface <|-- my_interface
  sc_prim_channel <|-- my_channel
  my_interface <|-- my_channel

docs.title: 1.3 Ports (Access Points)
docs.text:
• A port is a SystemC class templated by an interface type.
  • Declared as a data member inside a module.
  • Enables a module to invoke methods of a channel through the interface.
SC_MODULE(computation) {
  sc_port<my_interface> marks_po;
  sc_port<my_interface> grade_po;
  void compute();
  SC_CTOR(computation) { SC_THREAD(compute); }
};

docs.title: 2) Binding Ports and Channels
docs.text:
Steps: 1. Instantiate module(s). 2. Instantiate channel(s). 3. Bind port(s) to channel(s).

my_channel nc_marks, nc_grade;
computation comp("comp");
comp.marks_po(nc_marks);   // port bound to channel
comp.grade_po(nc_grade);
  • Ports behave like pointers to channels.
  • Channels must implement the interface required by the port.
flowchart LR
  M[Module] -->|port| P[sc_port]
  P -->|binds| C[Channel]
  C -->|implements| IF[Interface]

docs.title: 3) Example: Computation Module
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(computation) {
  sc_port<my_interface> marks_po, grade_po;
  void compute() {
    int m = marks_po->read();
    int g;
    if (m > 80) g = 9;
    else if (m > 60) g = 7;
    else g = 5;
    grade_po->write(g);
  }
  SC_CTOR(computation) { SC_THREAD(compute); }
};
  • The module does not know how data is stored in the channel.
  • It simply calls read() and write() on the port.
  • Encourages modularity and reusability.

docs.title: 4) sc_export
docs.text:
• sc_export<T> allows exposing a channel defined inside a module to the outside world.
  • Syntax similar to sc_port<T>.
SC_MODULE(M1) {
  sc_export<my_interface> e1;
  my_channel ch1;
  SC_CTOR(M1) : e1("e1") { e1(ch1); } // bind export to channel
};
  • External modules can now access M1's channel via the export.

docs.title: 5) Specialized Ports
docs.text:
• sc_in<T>: input port, exposes read(), event(), value_changed_event().
  • sc_out<T>: output port, exposes write().
  • sc_inout<T>: bidirectional.

Specialized for bool and sc_logic: - posedge_event(), negedge_event() → return event on transitions. - pos_edge(), neg_edge() → return boolean.

docs.title: 6) Example: Inverter Connection
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(INV) {
  sc_in<bool> A;
  sc_out<bool> Z;
  void compute(){
    while(1){
      Z.write(!A.read());
      wait(A.value_changed_event());
    }
  }
  SC_CTOR(INV) { SC_THREAD(compute); }
};

SC_MODULE(top) {
  sc_in<bool> A_top;
  sc_out<bool> Z_top;
  INV I1, I2;
  sc_signal<bool> s;
  SC_CTOR(top) : I1("I1"), I2("I2") {
    I1.A(A_top); I1.Z(s);
    I2.A(s); I2.Z(Z_top);
  }
};

flowchart LR
  A_top --> I1[INV] --> s[Signal] --> I2[INV] --> Z_top
  • Two inverters connected in series.
  • Signal s serves as an internal wire.

docs.title: 7) Testbench Construction
docs.text:
SC_MODULE(Testbench) {
  sc_signal<bool> s_in, v_out;
  top DUT;

  void apply_stimulus(){
    wait(SC_ZERO_TIME);
    s_in.write(true); wait(1, SC_SEC);
    s_in.write(false); wait(1, SC_SEC);
    s_in.write(true); wait(1, SC_SEC);
  }

  void report(){
    while(1){
      cout << "Input=" << s_in.read()
           << " Output=" << v_out.read()
           << " @ " << sc_time_stamp() << endl;
      wait(s_in.value_changed_event());
    }
  }

  SC_CTOR(Testbench) : DUT("top") {
    DUT.A_top(s_in);
    DUT.Z_top(v_out);
    SC_THREAD(apply_stimulus);
    SC_THREAD(report);
  }
};
  • Stimulus applied at different times.
  • Report process prints signal values during simulation.

docs.title: 8) Testbench Output
docs.text:
• After a few delta cycles, signals stabilize.
  • Useful for functional verification.
  • Can also dump waveforms to VCD for viewing.
Input=0 Output=1 @ 0 s
Input=1 Output=0 @ 1 s
Input=0 Output=1 @ 2 s
Input=1 Output=0 @ 3 s

docs.title: 9) Summary
docs.text:
• Interfaces: define abstract services.
  • Channels: implement interfaces and hold data/state.
  • Ports: allow modules to use interfaces without coupling.
  • Exports: expose internal channels externally.
  • Special ports: simplify signal-driven modeling.
  • Testbenches: simulate systems by applying input patterns and observing outputs.

docs.title: 10) References
docs.text: • Black, David C., and Jack Donovan, SystemC: From the ground up. Springer, 2004.

docs.title: Week 3 — Lecture 2: SystemC Communication and TLM
docs.text: Course: Advanced Digital Design and Verification Instructor: Sneh Saurabh • Date: 28 Aug 2025 Topic: SystemC Communication Primitives and Transaction-Level Modeling (TLM)

docs.title: 1) Channels in SystemC
docs.text:
Two types of channels:

Feature Primitive Channels (sc_prim_channel) Hierarchical Channels (sc_channel/sc_module) Ports & hierarchy No Yes Contains processes No Yes Purpose Simple & fast communication Complex bus-like modeling (PCI, AMBA, etc.) Examples sc_fifo<T>, sc_mutex, sc_semaphore Hierarchical buses 
graph TD
    Channels --> Primitive
    Channels --> Hierarchical
    Primitive --> sc_fifo
    Primitive --> sc_mutex
    Primitive --> sc_semaphore
    Hierarchical --> PCI
    Hierarchical --> AMBA

docs.title: 2) Mutual Exclusion — sc_mutex
docs.text:
• Provides exclusive access to shared resources.
  • Implements sc_mutex_if interface.
  • Member functions:
  • lock(): blocking acquire.
  • trylock(): non-blocking, returns 0 if locked.
  • unlock(): release.
SC_MODULE(ChangeRoom) {
  sc_mutex door;
  void customer_1_change();
  void customer_2_change();
  void customer_3_change();
  SC_CTOR(ChangeRoom) {
    SC_THREAD(customer_1_change);
    SC_THREAD(customer_2_change);
    SC_THREAD(customer_3_change);
  }
};

docs.title: 3) Resource Pooling — sc_semaphore
docs.text:
• Allows multiple processes to share a limited number of resources.
  • Implements sc_semaphore_if interface.
  • Member functions:
  • wait(): blocking acquire.
  • trywait(): non-blocking.
  • post(): release one resource.
  • get_value(): available slots.
SC_MODULE(Parking) {
  sc_semaphore slots;
  void car1();
  void car2();
  void car3();
  void car4();
  SC_CTOR(Parking) : slots(2) { // 2 slots available
    SC_THREAD(car1);
    SC_THREAD(car2);
    SC_THREAD(car3);
    SC_THREAD(car4);
  }
};

docs.title: 4) FIFO Queues — sc_fifo<T>
docs.text:
• First-in-first-out (FIFO) communication.
  • Implements sc_fifo_in_if<T> and sc_fifo_out_if<T>.
  • Member functions:
  • Writing: write(), nb_write(), data_write_event().
  • Reading: read(), nb_read(), data_read_event().
  • Query: num_available(), num_free().
SC_MODULE(TicketCounter) {
  sc_fifo<int> customers;
  void add_new_customer();
  void process_customer();
  SC_CTOR(TicketCounter) : customers(3) { // queue size 3
    SC_THREAD(add_new_customer);
    SC_THREAD(process_customer);
  }
};

docs.title: 5) Clock Channel — sc_clock
docs.text:
• Derived from sc_signal.
  • Models periodic clock signals.
  • Constructor: sc_clock(name, period, time_unit, duty_cycle, start_time, pos_edge_first).
sc_clock myclk("clk", 10, SC_NS, 0.5);

docs.title: Problem with HDL Models
docs.text:
• RTL/HDL simulate every cycle and every signal change.
  • Too detailed for high-level exploration.
  • Slows down system-level verification.

docs.title: TLM Approach
docs.text:
• Use function calls (transactions) instead of cycle-accurate signals.
  • 100–10,000x faster than RTL simulation.
flowchart LR
  RTL1[RTL Model] -->|Pin & cycle accurate| RTL2[RTL Model]
  FM1[Functional Model] -->|Function call| FM2[Functional Model]

docs.title: 7) TLM Applications
docs.text:
• Firmware/software development before RTL is ready.
  • Architectural modeling.
  • Performance analysis.
  • Functional verification.
graph TD
  TLM -->|fast| Software
  TLM -->|early| Architecture
  TLM -->|golden model| Verification

docs.title: 8) Timing Styles in TLM
docs.text:
• Loosely-timed (LT): whole transactions, fast, used in SW models.
  • Approximately-timed (AT): phase-based timing, more detailed.
  • Untimed (UT): no notion of time.
Style Detail Level Use Case UT None Functional verification LT Transaction SW perf analysis, architecture AT Phase-based HW perf analysis, verification

docs.title: 9) TLM-2.0 Overview
docs.text:
• Standardized by OSCI in 2005 (1.0) and 2008 (2.0).
  • Mechanisms:
  • Sockets: communication endpoints.
  • Generic payload: standard data container.
  • Blocking / non-blocking transport.
  • Direct Memory Interface (DMI).
  • Quantum keeper for timed simulations.

docs.title: 10) TLM Communication
docs.text:
• Socket: endpoint for communication.
  • Initiator: creates and sends transactions.
  • Target: receives and processes transactions.
sequenceDiagram
  participant Initiator
  participant Target
  Initiator->>Target: b_transport(payload)
  Target-->>Initiator: Response

docs.title: 11) Initiators and Targets
docs.text:
• Initiator socket: drives transactions.
  • Target socket: responds to transactions.
  • Interconnect can have many initiators and targets.
graph LR
  I[Initiator] --payload--> T[Target]
  T --response--> I
